content: Older prisoners are at a higher risk of victimization compared to their younger counterparts. Many prisoners expressed a desire for an increased presence of guards to enhance their protection. A study by Ravi et al. (2007) in the USA revealed that 65% of incarcerated women reported experiencing abuse prior to their imprisonment. This highlights the need for prison-based HIV prevention programs to address violence prevention, coping mechanisms, and the connection between HIV and violence. In 2009, three interventions were piloted in the USA to reduce violence in prisons. At Site A, an electronic system was implemented to monitor officers’ rounds, resulting in fewer reported instances of force. Site B installed cameras to reduce blind spots and record evidence for investigations, which led to a perception of reduced violence among inmates. At Site C, officers were trained in crisis intervention to improve interactions with inmates and prevent violent acts. Although the effectiveness at Site C could not be fully evaluated due to inmate housing restructuring, guards reported positive impressions of the training and recommended its expansion. In Australia, Yap et al. Changes included reducing the number of prisoners per cell, providing in-cell toilets and showers, increasing the number of cameras in various areas, employing roaming guards instead of stationary posts, and housing inmates based on risk levels. Additionally, guards were trained to emphasize their duty of care to victims of sexual assault and high-risk prisoners. HIV counseling and testing programs that are easily accessible upon prison entry and throughout incarceration have been shown to increase testing uptake. Confidentiality and voluntary participation are critical to the success of these programs. Mandatory testing and segregation policies are discouraged due to their counterproductive effects and potential negative health consequences. In Jamaica, a demonstration project offering mandatory opt-out testing for new prisoners and voluntary testing for those incarcerated for more than six months showed a high acceptance rate for voluntary testing (63%). Confidentiality and pre/post-test counseling were provided. In the USA, studies found that offering opt-out HIV testing within 24 hours of incarceration significantly increased testing rates among both male and female prisoners. Rapid testing was preferred by prison staff due to high turnover rates and was more effective in delivering results compared to conventional testing methods. Barriers to ART adherence in prisons include stigma, lack of privacy, insufficient nutritional support, and strained relationships with prison health staff. For example, the COMPASS program in Rhode Island linked HIV-positive inmates to care and social services, helping prevent drug relapse and improving retention in care after release. Needle and syringe exchange programs (NSPs) in prisons have been effective in reducing needle-sharing and associated HIV infections. These programs also reduce overdose risks and facilitate referrals to drug dependence treatment. Evidence suggests that NSPs do not increase drug use and improve hygienic conditions in prisons. Comprehensive HIV prevention programs in prisons should include education, condom distribution, needle exchange programs, drug dependence treatment, and access to antiretroviral therapy (ART). Ensuring continuity of care from the community to prison and back is critical for successful treatment outcomes. In summary, addressing HIV prevention, treatment, and care in prisons requires a multifaceted approach that includes education, stigma reduction, access to testing and treatment, and continuity of care.
